title: CHAPTER 9: HISTORY OF ODISHA – MEDIEVAL PERIOD

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Gajapati Kingdom was established in the 15th century by Kapilendra Deva, marking a golden era in medieval Odia history.
Chaitanya Mahaprabhu spent his final years in Puri, significantly impacting the Vaishnavism tradition and culture in Odisha.
With the defeat of Mukunda Deva in 1568, Odisha lost its independence and came under Afghan, followed by Mughal rule.
The Marathas established their rule over Odisha in the mid-18th century, maintaining control until the British takeover.

blocks.content: The Gajapati dynasty succeeded the Eastern Gangas and ruled Odisha from Cuttack. Kapilendradeva (1435–1467) was the greatest Gajapati ruler who extended the empire from the Ganga in the north to the Kaveri in the south.

rows: Patronage and protection of Jagannath Temple

blocks.content: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the Vaishnava saint from Bengal, came to Puri and spent 18 years (1510–1533) at Jagannath Puri. His influence greatly shaped Odisha's Vaishnavism and the Jagannath cult. The panchasabda (five musical instruments) tradition of Jagannath Temple is associated with this period.

After the decline of the Gajapatis, the Afghan rulers (Sulaiman Karrani) conquered Odisha in 1568. The Mughals under Akbar's general Man Singh captured Odisha in 1592. The Subah of Odisha was established as a Mughal province. During this period, the Jagannath cult suffered but also persisted.

items: Kapilendra Deva was the founder of the Suryavamsi Gajapati Dynasty.
1568 AD is considered a watershed year in Odisha history due to the fall of the independent Hindu kingdom to Sulaiman Karrani's forces.
Questions often ask about the patron king of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in Odisha, who was Prataparudra Deva.

blocks.content: The Marathas conquered Odisha in 1751 and it remained under Maratha (Bhonsle of Nagpur) control until 1803. During Maratha rule, the Jagannath Temple was restored. Revenue was collected through the panda system. The Maratha rule is remembered for its extractive nature.
